patch_notes.summary: Additive aggregate-review expansion. Adds 8 subgenre terms and 5 tone tags, clarifies documentary and sitcom boundaries, retains every v0.2.0 controlled ID, and corrects stale v0.2.0 count metadata.
motivation: The 2,000-title aggregate review produced 31 editorial override candidates: 10 biographical/profile works forced into documentary, 11 scripted true-crime works forced into documentary, 6 medical dramas reduced to generic workplace or procedural labels, and 4 films incorrectly assigned the TV-only family-sitcom term.

Low-confidence and recommended-review cases also exposed missing vocabulary for comic fantasy or supernatural works, paranormal suspense that is not primarily horror, and concert or music-performance films that are not music documentaries.

The tone distribution repeatedly collapsed diffuse nervousness into tense, physical attraction into romantic, frank disclosure into earnest or gritty, high-energy joy into playful or uplifting, and backward-looking affection into melancholic or sentimental.
patch_notes.compatibility: All 130 v0.2.0 subgenre IDs, all 28 v0.2.0 tone IDs, and all pacing IDs are retained. Only boundary guidance for the four listed existing terms changed; no existing ID was renamed or retired.

purpose: Classifies intrinsic editorial properties of a movie or TV show: what kind of work it is (subgenre), its emotional register (tone), and its narrative rhythm (pacing). Excludes derived or externally sourced signals such as hidden-gem status, comfort-watch status, rewatchability, mainstream/niche positioning, film-school-worthiness, canonical importance, or Criterion status.
animation_design_principle: Animation is primarily a medium, not a genre. Do not force every animated or anime title into an Animation-family term. Prefer an existing, more specific non-animation subgenre as primary whenever it accurately describes the work's content (e.g. an animated superhero film should still classify as superhero; an animated romantic comedy should still classify as romantic-comedy). Animation-family terms exist for the residual cases where the animation-specific convention itself — not just the medium — is the meaningful editorial signal.

fields.primary_subgenre: Exactly one controlled subgenre id. The single most useful, specific answer to 'what kind of work is this?'
fields.secondary_subgenre: Zero or one controlled subgenre id. Must differ from primary_subgenre. Optional.
fields.tone_tags: Zero to three controlled tone ids. Prefer exactly three whenever three genuinely descriptive, non-redundant controlled tone ids apply. Two is acceptable only when a third would be weak, redundant, speculative, or misleading. One or zero should be rare, reserved for genuinely insufficient evidence. Never pad to three simply to hit the preferred count. Three remains the maximum. See `tone_tag_preference_policy` below.
fields.pacing: One of slow | moderate | fast, or null if there is insufficient evidence.

terms.label: Romantic Comedy
terms.definition: A comedy centered on the development of a romantic relationship, typically resolving with the couple's union.

terms.label: Dark Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy that plays traditionally serious or taboo subject matter (death, illness, crime) for laughs while keeping a recognizably comic tone throughout.

terms.label: Black Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy built around a bleak, morbid, or misanthropic worldview, where humor and disturbing content are inseparable rather than one offsetting the other.

terms.label: Screwball Comedy
terms.definition: Fast-talking, farcical comedy of mismatched romantic pairs, class conflict, or social role reversal, marked by rapid-fire dialogue and escalating misunderstandings.

terms.label: Satire
terms.definition: Comedy that uses irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to critique a specific real-world target such as institutions, politics, public figures, or social norms.

terms.label: Parody / Spoof
terms.definition: Comedy built by directly imitating and exaggerating the conventions of a specific genre, film, or franchise for comic effect.

terms.label: Workplace Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy centered on the dynamics, hierarchy, and absurdities of a specific job or workplace.

terms.label: Coming-of-Age Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy centered on a young protagonist's transition toward adulthood, told primarily through humor.

terms.label: Buddy Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy driven by the mismatched-pair dynamic between two (or more) friends or partners thrown together by circumstance.

terms.label: Breakup Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy centered on the end of a romantic relationship and its comic fallout.

terms.label: Sex Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy in which sexual pursuit, desire, or awkwardness is the primary comic engine.

terms.label: Stoner Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy centered on drug use, typically cannabis, as a defining lifestyle and source of episodic, low-stakes misadventure.

terms.label: Absurdist Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy built on illogical premises or a fundamentally irrational world, where the humor comes from that irrationality itself.

terms.label: Mockumentary
terms.definition: Comedy that adopts documentary form (interviews, handheld footage, narration) as a fictional device.

terms.label: Family Comedy
terms.definition: Feature-length or otherwise non-sitcom comedy centered on a family household, intergenerational conflict, or a family misadventure as its primary comic engine.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use for live-action or mixed-format films whose comedy is organized around family relationships, including broad all-ages farce, body-swap stories, and escalating household mishaps.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use as a generic audience-rating label. For a recurring episodic household comedy use family-sitcom; for an animated work whose family-audience convention matters more than its comic construction use animated-family.

terms.label: Slapstick Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy in which physical mishaps, pratfalls, collisions, chases, destruction, or exaggerated bodily action supply a dominant and recurring share of the humor.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use when physical action is a defining comic construction rather than an occasional gag; it can pair with family-comedy, parody-spoof, or another premise term.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not infer slapstick merely because a comedy contains one chase, accident, or clumsy character.

terms.label: Observational Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up built primarily from close observations of everyday behavior, relationships, routines, or social conventions.

terms.label: Storytelling Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up organized around extended personal or reported stories whose narrative development and payoff are central to the act.

terms.label: Satirical Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up that sustains critique of politics, institutions, ideologies, public figures, or social norms through ridicule, irony, or exaggeration.

terms.label: Dark Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up that repeatedly turns death, trauma, illness, cruelty, or other taboo and distressing subjects into its primary comic material.

terms.label: Deadpan Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up whose defining performance technique is controlled, flat, or affectless delivery that contrasts with the material.

terms.label: Absurdist Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up driven by surreal premises, non sequiturs, anti-logic, or deliberately irrational escalation rather than ordinary realism.

terms.label: Raunchy Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up in which explicit sexual, bodily, or profane material is a dominant and recurring comic engine.

terms.label: One-Liner Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up structured around a high density of short, self-contained jokes rather than extended narratives or thematic passages.

terms.label: Alternative Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up that deliberately rejects conventional setup-and-punchline presentation through experimental structure, anti-comedy, multimedia, or performance-art techniques.

terms.label: Character Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up built substantially around original personas or sustained fictional characters performed by the comedian.

terms.label: Musical Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up in which original songs, musical performance, or music-driven routines are integral to the comedy rather than incidental accompaniment.

terms.label: Clean Stand-Up
terms.definition: Stand-up deliberately designed to avoid explicit sexual content and strong profanity as a defining audience and performance choice; do not infer it merely from missing evidence.

terms.label: Prop Comedy
terms.definition: Stand-up in which physical objects, visual devices, or constructed stage gimmicks are essential to a substantial share of the jokes.

terms.label: Impressions
terms.definition: Stand-up in which vocal or physical imitation of recognizable people, celebrities, or character types is a dominant performance technique.

terms.label: Family Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on the relationships, conflicts, and obligations within a family unit.

terms.label: Relationship Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on an intimate relationship between a small number of characters, without primarily being a romance in the genre sense.

terms.label: Psychological Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on a character's internal mental or emotional state as the primary source of conflict.

terms.label: Legal Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on the practice of law, including litigation, legal ethics, or the justice system, told from a legal-professional point of view.

terms.label: Political Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on the pursuit, exercise, or consequences of political power.

terms.label: Historical Drama
terms.definition: Drama set in a clearly defined past era where the historical setting materially shapes the story (period drama).

terms.label: Social Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on a social issue or systemic condition, such as poverty, addiction, or discrimination, and its effect on characters' lives.

terms.label: Workplace Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on the stakes, hierarchy, and pressures of a specific job or workplace, without comic framing.

terms.label: Coming-of-Age Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on a young protagonist's transition toward adulthood or self-understanding.

terms.label: Sports Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on athletic competition, training, or a sports institution as the primary stakes.

terms.label: Showbiz Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on the entertainment industry and the toll or mechanics of fame and creative work.

terms.label: Biographical Drama
terms.definition: Scripted narrative that dramatizes the life, career, or defining period of a real person or small group, using actors, constructed scenes, and dramatic storytelling.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use for biopics and scripted profile miniseries even when events are compressed or fictionalized for drama.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Use biography-profile-documentary for nonfiction profiles built primarily from interviews, observation, reporting, or archival evidence. If a real criminal case rather than a person's broader life is the central organizing subject, prefer true-crime-drama.

terms.label: Medical Drama
terms.definition: Scripted drama centered on clinicians, patients, treatment decisions, or the institutional pressures of medicine, with medical work materially structuring the story.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use for hospital, clinic, emergency-response, and mental-health-care dramas whether serialized or case-based; procedural may be secondary when episode structure warrants it.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use when illness is only a character circumstance or when a hospital is incidental to a story whose defining engine lies elsewhere.

terms.label: Crime Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on the commission, investigation, or consequences of crime, without being primarily a thriller, procedural, or heist.

terms.label: Gangster
terms.definition: Story centered on the rise and/or fall of an individual criminal figure within a criminal underworld or hierarchy.

terms.label: Heist
terms.definition: Story structured around the planning and execution of a theft or robbery.

terms.label: Detective
terms.definition: Story centered on an investigator, professional or amateur, solving a case, with the investigative process as the narrative engine.

terms.label: Police Procedural
terms.definition: Story centered on law enforcement's routine methods and casework, emphasizing process over the personal drama of any one case.

terms.label: Neo-Noir
terms.definition: Contemporary story that consciously adopts classic film-noir conventions, such as moral ambiguity and a shadowy visual and narrative tone, in a modern or non-period setting.

terms.label: Courtroom Crime
terms.definition: Crime story structured primarily around trial proceedings rather than investigation.

terms.label: Organized Crime
terms.definition: Story centered on the operations, politics, or culture of a criminal organization as an institution, distinct from a single gangster's rise-and-fall arc.

terms.label: True Crime Drama
terms.definition: Scripted dramatization of a documented real crime, criminal investigation, trial, or case, using actors and constructed narrative scenes rather than documentary presentation.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use when the work's identity depends on reenacting or dramatizing a specific real case, including dramatized miniseries and narrative films.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Use true-crime-documentary for nonfiction reporting, interviews, archival evidence, or observational case coverage. Use crime-drama when the story is fictional or merely loosely inspired by real events.

terms.label: Psychological Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller driven by uncertainty about a character's mental state, perception, or trustworthiness rather than by physical danger alone.

terms.label: Crime Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller organized around a criminal act or criminal antagonist, prioritizing suspense and pursuit over procedural or investigative detail.

terms.label: Political Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller in which political power, conspiracy, or state institutions create the central danger.

terms.label: Conspiracy Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller centered on a protagonist uncovering a hidden, coordinated plot, typically involving institutions working against them.

terms.label: Espionage Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller centered on intelligence work, spies, or covert operations.

terms.label: Erotic Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller in which sexual desire or a sexual relationship is the mechanism that generates danger or suspense.

terms.label: Tech Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller in which technology, such as surveillance, AI, hacking, or engineered systems, is the central source of threat or the primary tool of danger.

terms.label: Survival Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller centered on a character's struggle to physically survive a hostile environment or antagonist, with escape or endurance as the core stakes.

terms.label: Revenge Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller structured around a protagonist's pursuit of retribution against those who wronged them.

terms.label: Supernatural Thriller
terms.definition: Thriller whose central danger, pursuit, or conspiracy is driven by a paranormal or occult force, while suspense and escalating jeopardy matter more than sustained fear or horror imagery.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use for occult investigations, supernatural conspiracies, dangerous hauntings, curses, or ritual threats structured primarily through suspense.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Use supernatural-horror when frightening the audience is the dominant mode, dark-fantasy when fantastical worldbuilding or quest structure dominates, and mystery-thriller when the apparently paranormal element is incidental or ultimately non-supernatural.

terms.label: Action-Thriller
terms.definition: Action-forward story that also sustains thriller-level suspense and stakes, blending set-piece spectacle with mounting tension.

terms.label: Martial Arts
terms.definition: Action centered on hand-to-hand combat systems or disciplines as a primary visual and narrative focus.

terms.label: Adventure Action
terms.definition: Action built around a journey, quest, or exploration, prioritizing spectacle and momentum over emotional interiority.

terms.label: Military Action
terms.definition: Action centered on organized armed forces, combat units, or military operations.

terms.label: Superhero
terms.definition: Action centered on a character or team with extraordinary powers or abilities operating within a superhero mythology or universe.

terms.label: Revenge Action
terms.definition: Action structured around a protagonist's violent retribution against those who wronged them, with action set pieces as the primary means of pursuing it.

terms.label: Disaster
terms.definition: Action centered on characters surviving a large-scale catastrophic event, natural or man-made.

terms.label: Psychological Horror
terms.definition: Horror that generates fear through mental deterioration, unreliable perception, or dread rather than explicit monsters or violence.

terms.label: Supernatural Horror
terms.definition: Horror in which the threat originates from a paranormal or otherworldly force, such as ghosts, demons, or possession.

terms.label: Folk Horror
terms.definition: Horror rooted in isolated communities, rural landscapes, or pre-modern belief systems and rituals.

terms.label: Body Horror
terms.definition: Horror centered on the graphic transformation, mutilation, or violation of the human body.

terms.label: Slasher
terms.definition: Horror structured around a killer stalking and murdering a sequence of victims, typically with a signature method or weapon.

terms.label: Creature Feature
terms.definition: Horror centered on a monster or creature as the primary physical antagonist.

terms.label: Gothic Horror
terms.definition: Horror built on atmosphere, decayed grandeur, and classic gothic settings such as mansions, castles, and family curses, over graphic violence.

terms.label: Cosmic Horror
terms.definition: Horror centered on incomprehensible, vast, or indifferent forces beyond human understanding or control.

terms.label: Horror-Comedy
terms.definition: Horror that plays its scares for comic effect, alternating or blending fear and humor as co-equal tones.

terms.label: Survival Horror
terms.definition: Horror centered on a character's physical struggle to survive a hostile threat or environment, emphasizing endurance over investigation.

terms.label: Sci-Fi Horror
terms.definition: Horror in which the source of threat is grounded in science-fiction premises, such as aliens, experiments, or technology gone wrong.

terms.label: Hard Sci-Fi
terms.definition: Science fiction that emphasizes scientific plausibility and technical accuracy as central to the story's logic and stakes.

terms.label: Dystopian Sci-Fi
terms.definition: Science fiction set in an oppressive or degraded future society, centered on that society's control over its people.

terms.label: Cyberpunk
terms.definition: Science fiction combining advanced technology, often digital or cybernetic, with social decay, corporate power, and a stylized urban underworld.

terms.label: Space Opera
terms.definition: Science fiction centered on large-scale adventure across space, typically with sweeping stakes, multiple factions, or galactic scope.

terms.label: Alien First Contact
terms.definition: Science fiction centered on humanity's encounter or communication with a non-human extraterrestrial intelligence.

terms.label: Time Travel
terms.definition: Science fiction structured around movement between different points in time as the central narrative mechanic.

terms.label: Tech Sci-Fi
terms.definition: Science fiction centered on the near-term social or personal consequences of a specific emerging technology.

terms.label: Post-Apocalyptic
terms.definition: Science fiction set after a civilization-ending event, centered on survival in its aftermath.

terms.label: Epic Fantasy
terms.definition: Fantasy set in an original secondary world with large-scale stakes, sprawling scope, and mythic structure.

terms.label: Dark Fantasy
terms.definition: Fantasy that foregrounds horror elements, moral bleakness, or menace within its fantastical world.

terms.label: Urban Fantasy
terms.definition: Fantasy in which magical or mythical elements exist within a recognizably contemporary, real-world setting.

terms.label: Magical Realism
terms.definition: Story grounded in a realistic, everyday setting where a small number of magical elements are treated as unremarkable by the characters.

terms.label: Fairy Tale / Fable
terms.definition: Story structured as or directly adapted from a traditional fairy tale, fable, or folk tale, retaining that form's moral or symbolic logic.

terms.label: Sword and Sorcery
terms.definition: Fantasy centered on a physically capable individual hero or small band navigating personal-scale battles against magical or monstrous threats, prioritizing action over world-spanning stakes.

terms.label: Fantasy / Supernatural Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy whose primary comic engine depends on magic, ghosts, demons, mythic beings, body-swapping, curses, or another impossible supernatural premise.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use when removing the fantastical or paranormal premise would remove the work's defining jokes, situations, or character dynamics.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Use horror-comedy when horror conventions and scares remain co-dominant, romantic-comedy when romance drives the structure and magic is incidental, and family-comedy when family misadventure rather than the fantasy device is primary.

terms.label: Romantic Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on a romantic relationship where the relationship's course, not its comic potential, drives the story.

terms.label: Period Romance
terms.definition: Romance set in a clearly defined historical era where the setting's social conventions materially shape the relationship.

terms.label: Tragic Romance
terms.definition: Romance in which the central relationship is defined by its failure, loss, or the death or separation of one or both partners.

terms.label: Erotic Romance
terms.definition: Romance in which sexual desire and intimacy are a central, foregrounded element of the relationship's portrayal.

terms.label: Murder Mystery
terms.definition: Mystery organized around solving a specific killing, with the culprit's identity as the central question.

terms.label: Whodunit
terms.definition: Mystery structured as a formal puzzle with a defined set of suspects, clues, and a fair-play reveal of the culprit.

terms.label: Mystery-Thriller
terms.definition: Mystery that sustains thriller-level tension and danger alongside its central puzzle, rather than proceeding at a purely investigative pace.

terms.label: Puzzle Mystery
terms.definition: Mystery centered on solving a complex structural or intellectual puzzle, not necessarily a crime, as the core engine.

terms.label: Combat Film
terms.definition: War story centered on frontline combat and its physical experience.

terms.label: Anti-War Film
terms.definition: War story whose primary purpose is to critique the morality, cost, or futility of war itself.

terms.label: POW / Escape
terms.definition: War story centered on captivity and a prisoner-of-war's attempt to escape or endure imprisonment.

terms.label: Home-Front War Drama
terms.definition: War story centered on civilians or communities affected by a war occurring elsewhere.

terms.label: Traditional Western
terms.definition: Western that upholds classic genre conventions, such as clear moral lines, frontier justice, and iconic Old West setting, without substantially subverting them.

terms.label: Revisionist Western
terms.definition: Western that consciously subverts or critiques classic genre conventions, complicating its moral framework or mythology.

terms.label: Neo-Western
terms.definition: Western sensibility and themes relocated to a modern-day setting.

terms.label: Traditional Musical
terms.definition: Story in which characters break into song-and-dance numbers as a core, integrated storytelling device.

terms.label: Music Drama
terms.definition: Drama centered on musicians, music-making, or the music industry, without characters performing full musical numbers as a narrative device.

terms.label: Music Comedy
terms.definition: Comedy centered on musicians, music-making, or the music industry, without characters performing full musical numbers as a narrative device.

terms.label: Concert Film / Music Performance
terms.definition: Nonfiction film or special whose primary purpose is to present a live or deliberately staged musical performance, with the performance itself occupying most of the work.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use for captured concerts, tour films dominated by complete performances, and staged music-performance specials; limited backstage material does not disqualify it.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Use music-documentary when interviews, history, biography, or behind-the-scenes explanation are the primary structure. Use traditional-musical for a fictional narrative told through integrated songs.

terms.label: Investigative Documentary
terms.definition: Documentary structured around uncovering previously hidden or disputed facts about its subject.

terms.label: Biography / Profile Documentary
terms.definition: Nonfiction work that profiles the life of a real person or small group through interviews, observation, reporting, archival evidence, or other documentary material.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use for scripted reenactment or actor-led dramatization of a real life; use biographical-drama instead.

terms.label: Political / Social Documentary
terms.definition: Documentary centered on a political issue, policy, or broad social phenomenon.

terms.label: Nature Documentary
terms.definition: Documentary centered on the natural world, wildlife, or the environment.

terms.label: Music Documentary
terms.definition: Nonfiction work that interprets or documents a musician, band, music scene, career, or history primarily through interviews, observation, reporting, or archival evidence.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Use concert-film when presenting sustained musical performance is the work's primary purpose rather than contextualizing the artist or music.

terms.label: Sports Documentary
terms.definition: Documentary centered on an athlete, team, or sporting event or era.

terms.label: True Crime Documentary
terms.definition: Nonfiction work that examines a real crime, investigation, trial, or criminal case through reporting, interviews, observation, or archival evidence.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use for scripted reenactment or actor-led dramatization of a real case; use true-crime-drama instead.

terms.label: Sitcom
terms.definition: Half-hour-scale scripted comedy built around a recurring ensemble and self-contained episodic situations, with a stable premise across episodes.

terms.label: Workplace Sitcom
terms.definition: Sitcom whose recurring setting and ensemble are organized around a specific workplace.

terms.label: Family Sitcom
terms.definition: Recurring episodic sitcom whose stable setting and ensemble are organized around a family household.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use for a feature film or one-off special centered on family mishaps; use family-comedy, optionally paired with slapstick-comedy or fantasy-comedy.

terms.label: Dramedy
terms.definition: Series that deliberately sustains both comedic and dramatic registers as co-equal tones across episodes, rather than one dominating.

terms.label: Procedural
terms.definition: Episodic series structured around a self-contained case, incident, or problem resolved largely within each episode.

terms.label: Prestige Drama
terms.definition: Serialized hour-long drama with heightened production values and creative ambition, built for sustained arcs across a season rather than episodic cases.

terms.label: Soap / Serial Drama
terms.definition: Serialized drama centered on interpersonal melodrama across an ensemble, with long-running, heavily plotted relationship arcs.

terms.label: Anthology
terms.definition: Series in which each season or episode tells a self-contained story with a new setting and/or cast, connected by theme rather than continuing plot.

terms.label: Sketch Comedy
terms.definition: Series built from a sequence of short, unconnected comedic sketches rather than a continuing story or ensemble situation.

terms.label: Reality Competition
terms.definition: Unscripted series structured around contestants competing toward elimination or a defined prize.

terms.label: Docuseries
terms.definition: Multi-episode nonfiction series following a real subject, event, or investigation across a season.

terms.label: Late-Night Talk Show
terms.definition: Recurring host-driven program built around a nightly or daily format of monologues, celebrity interviews, and comedic segments.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use for programs structured around a recurring host, guest interviews, and monologue or comedy-segment format, regardless of exact airtime.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Distinct from sketch-comedy: sketch-comedy is built from a sequence of unconnected scripted sketches with no recurring host-interview structure. Distinct from news-satire: news-satire's comedic structure is built specifically around parodying news-broadcast conventions and current events rather than general celebrity interviews, even though both formats may share a nightly airtime.
anchor_titles: The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon
The Late Show with Stephen Colbert

terms.label: News Satire
terms.definition: Program structured around satirizing current news and events specifically, using a news-broadcast format (anchor desk, correspondents, headlines) as the comedic vehicle.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use when the show's comedic structure is specifically built around parodying news-broadcast conventions and current events, not general celebrity interviews.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Distinct from satire (Comedy family): satire is a general-purpose critique of any real-world target through irony or exaggeration, in any format (film, sitcom, etc.), while news-satire specifically names the news-broadcast-format vehicle. Distinct from late-night-talk-show: a news-satire program is organized around news headlines and correspondents rather than a monologue-plus-celebrity-interview structure.

terms.label: Animated Family
terms.definition: Animated work made primarily for a general or family audience, where the all-ages, gentle sensibility itself is a meaningful editorial signal beyond genre or plot content.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use as primary when no existing non-animation subgenre captures the work's content precisely (e.g. a gentle, low-plot family adventure). Use as secondary when an existing subgenre (adventure-action, epic-fantasy, superhero, etc.) already captures the content precisely but the all-ages animated packaging is still a materially useful signal for a viewer choosing what to watch.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not apply merely because a title is animated — animation is a medium, not automatically a subgenre. Skip this tag when the all-ages framing adds no information beyond what the existing primary subgenre already conveys. Do not use for adult-oriented animation (see adult-animation).
anchor_titles: Snoopy Presents: There's No Place Like Home, Snoopy

terms.label: Adult Animation
terms.definition: Animated work created for and marketed to an adult audience, typically featuring mature humor, themes, or content not intended for a general family audience.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use when the adult-oriented intent of the animation is itself a meaningful signal — for satirical adult sitcoms, adult sci-fi comedy, and similar — as primary if no other subgenre fits, or as secondary alongside a precise content subgenre (e.g. family-sitcom, absurdist-comedy).
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not apply to all-ages or family-targeted animation (see animated-family). Do not apply merely because a title contains some crude humor if it remains fundamentally family-marketed. This term flags audience intent, not a specific comedic genre — pair it with the actual content subgenre (satire, family-sitcom, absurdist-comedy, etc.) rather than using it alone whenever a more specific fit exists.

terms.label: Anime Action
terms.definition: Japanese-animation (anime) work whose primary appeal is fast-paced physical or supernatural combat, told through anime-specific genre conventions such as shonen tournament arcs, power escalation, or creature-battling structures.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use as primary when the anime genre conventions themselves — not just the fact of being Japanese-animated — are the meaningful classification signal, e.g. a shonen battle series or creature-battling tournament adventure.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use simply because a title is Japanese-animated, and do not use for a Western production merely styled after anime (an "anime-inspired" visual aesthetic is not the same as being part of the anime industry/tradition). If an existing non-animation subgenre (cyberpunk, martial-arts, superhero, adventure-action) already captures the content precisely, prefer that as primary and use anime-action only as a secondary flag if the anime-specific conventions add real information. Distinct from martial-arts (existing; discipline-focused combat, not anime-specific).

terms.label: Isekai
terms.definition: Anime or anime-adjacent work in which a protagonist is transported, reincarnated, or otherwise displaced into a different, typically fantasy or game-like, world, and that displacement premise structures the story.
terms.inclusion_guidance: Use when the isekai displacement premise (death-and-reincarnation, portal transport, or being pulled into a game world) is itself a defining structural element of the plot.
terms.exclusion_guidance: Do not use as a generic synonym for "characters travel to another world" — a Western portal-fantasy story should use urban-fantasy or epic-fantasy instead. Isekai names a specific anime genre convention, not a plot device available to any medium. If the work is anime but not built around a displacement premise, prefer anime-action or an existing fantasy subgenre instead.

tone_tags.label: Warm
tone_tags.definition: Conveys genuine affection, kindness, or emotional closeness between characters; the viewer feels comforted by the relationships on screen.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as uplifting: warm describes the emotional temperature of relationships, not the trajectory or resolution of the story. A story can be warm and still end sadly.

tone_tags.label: Bittersweet
tone_tags.definition: Blends genuine happiness or resolution with an equally genuine sense of loss, so that neither feeling cancels the other out.
tone_tags.not: Not simply a sad story with a happy ending: in bittersweet work the joy and the loss are both fully present at once, rather than joy following after sadness has passed.

tone_tags.label: Melancholic
tone_tags.definition: A persistent, low-intensity sadness or wistfulness that colors the work without dominating it or removing hope entirely.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from bleak: melancholic sadness is reflective and survivable, and can coexist with warmth or gentle humor; bleak withholds hope almost entirely.

tone_tags.label: Bleak
tone_tags.definition: Portrays a world or outcome with little to no meaningful hope, comfort, or redemption; despair is the dominant, unresolved note.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from melancholic: bleak work offers little or no relief from despair, where melancholic allows sadness to coexist with warmth, humor, or reflection.

tone_tags.label: Uplifting
tone_tags.definition: Leaves the viewer with a sense of hope, affirmation, or emotional lift, typically through the story's trajectory or resolution.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as warm: uplifting describes the emotional arc or destination of the story, not the texture of relationships throughout it. A hard-won triumph can be uplifting without being warm.

tone_tags.label: Sentimental
tone_tags.definition: Deliberately and openly appeals to tender emotion, often through music, dialogue, or framing designed to elicit feeling.
tone_tags.not: Not neutral about its emotional intent: sentimental work wears its heartstring-pulling openly, unlike warm or bittersweet work that earns emotion more obliquely.

tone_tags.label: Playful
tone_tags.definition: Light, mischievous, and energetic in spirit; takes evident delight in its own game, characters, or premise.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as absurdist: playful describes an inviting, high-spirited energy, while absurdist specifically involves illogic or a fundamentally irrational premise.

tone_tags.label: Raunchy
tone_tags.definition: Explicit, crude, or graphic in its sexual or bodily humor, foregrounded as a deliberate comic engine rather than incidental content.
tone_tags.not: Not simply 'contains adult content': raunchy specifically means crude sexual or bodily material is a deliberate comic device, not background material in a serious drama.

tone_tags.label: Deadpan
tone_tags.definition: Delivered with flat, affectless line readings or reactions, where the humor comes from the gap between that flat delivery and outrageous or absurd content.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from wry: deadpan is a performance or delivery style (flat affect), while wry is a narrative attitude of dry, knowing understatement that doesn't require flat performance.
anchor_titles: What We Do in the Shadows

tone_tags.label: Absurdist
tone_tags.definition: Built on illogical premises or a fundamentally irrational world where normal cause-and-effect or social logic doesn't apply.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as playful: absurdist is about the internal logic, or lack of it, governing the story's world, not simply a lighthearted mood.

tone_tags.label: Satirical
tone_tags.definition: Critiques a specific real-world target, such as institutions, public figures, ideologies, or social norms, through irony or exaggeration.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from cynical: satirical implies an active, pointed critique aimed at a specific target, while cynical is a general distrustful stance with no particular object of ridicule.

tone_tags.label: Wry
tone_tags.definition: A dry, understated, knowing sense of humor communicated through attitude and tone rather than performance style or premise.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from deadpan: wry is an authorial or narrative attitude of dry amusement, while deadpan refers specifically to flat delivery or performance.

tone_tags.label: Tense
tone_tags.definition: Sustains anticipatory anxiety about what might happen next; the viewer feels suspense about an uncertain outcome.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from menacing: tense is about uncertainty and anticipation, asking whether something bad will happen, while menacing is about the felt presence of a specific threatening force, even without uncertainty about the outcome.

tone_tags.label: Menacing
tone_tags.definition: Conveys the felt presence of a specific threatening force, person, or entity, regardless of whether the outcome is in doubt.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from tense: menacing describes a quality radiating from a person, place, or force, not the viewer's uncertainty about the plot's outcome.

tone_tags.label: Unsettling
tone_tags.definition: Produces a diffuse sense of wrongness or discomfort that resists clear explanation, unmoored from a specific identifiable threat.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from menacing: unsettling doesn't require a locatable source of danger; the discomfort itself, not a specific threat, is the point.

tone_tags.label: Visceral
tone_tags.definition: Produces an immediate, bodily reaction in the viewer through violence, physical intensity, or sensory extremity.
tone_tags.not: Not simply 'intense' in an abstract sense: visceral specifically implies a physical, gut-level reaction rather than an intellectual or purely emotional one.

tone_tags.label: Cerebral
tone_tags.definition: Prioritizes ideas, logic, or intellectual engagement, asking the viewer to actively think through concepts or implications.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from enigmatic: cerebral work can be fully explicable and resolved, just demanding, while enigmatic work specifically withholds clear meaning or resolution.

tone_tags.label: Enigmatic
tone_tags.definition: Deliberately withholds clear meaning, explanation, or resolution, leaving significant ambiguity intact by design.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from cerebral: enigmatic is defined by unresolved ambiguity itself, not by the amount of thinking required. A work can be cerebral and still fully resolve its ideas.

tone_tags.label: Meditative
tone_tags.definition: Unhurried and contemplative, favoring stillness, reflection, or atmosphere over incident, inviting the viewer to sit with a mood or idea.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as slow pacing alone: meditative describes an emotional and tonal register of quiet reflection, though it frequently co-occurs with slow pacing.

tone_tags.label: Dreamlike
tone_tags.definition: Evokes the logic, imagery, or atmosphere of a dream: fluid, associative, and not bound by strict realism or causality.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from enigmatic: dreamlike is about atmosphere and the loosening of realistic logic, not necessarily about withholding meaning or resolution.

tone_tags.label: Gritty
tone_tags.definition: Depicts its world with unvarnished, tactile realism: grime, hardship, and consequence rendered without glamorization.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as bleak: gritty is about the texture and realism of the depiction, not the presence or absence of hope in the story's outcome.

tone_tags.label: Stylized
tone_tags.definition: Foregrounds a distinctive, heightened visual or formal aesthetic that departs from naturalism as a deliberate authorial choice.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as dreamlike: stylized refers to a consciously crafted aesthetic choice, which can be sharp and precise rather than fluid or associative.

tone_tags.label: Earnest
tone_tags.definition: Sincere and direct in its emotional or moral intent, without irony, cynicism, or a protective wink to the audience.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from sentimental: earnest describes sincerity of intent, not the deployment of tear-jerking technique. A work can be earnest without being emotionally manipulative.

tone_tags.label: Cynical
tone_tags.definition: Assumes and portrays self-interested or corrupt motives as the default, distrustful of institutions, sincerity, or good intentions.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from satirical: cynical is a general worldview or stance, while satirical requires an active, pointed critique of a specific target.

tone_tags.label: Romantic
tone_tags.definition: Foregrounds longing, attraction, or love as an idealized emotional force driving the work's central feeling.
tone_tags.not: Not the same as sentimental: romantic describes the specific object of feeling, love or desire, while sentimental describes an emotionally manipulative technique that can apply to any subject.

tone_tags.label: Thoughtful
tone_tags.definition: Reflective and self-aware, using the performance to consider lived experience or ideas in a way meant to linger beyond the immediate joke.

tone_tags.label: Inventive
tone_tags.definition: Feels formally imaginative or structurally novel in an observable way; use for unusual construction or presentation, not as generic praise for creativity.

tone_tags.label: Surprising
tone_tags.definition: Repeatedly subverts the audience's expectations through unexpected turns, reveals, reversals, or punchlines; a single twist is insufficient.

tone_tags.label: Anxious
tone_tags.definition: Creates a persistent, agitated sense of nervousness, social pressure, or unease that need not center on a single impending outcome.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from tense: tense is suspense about what will happen next, while anxious describes diffuse nervous activation that can persist even when no discrete threat or outcome is pending.

tone_tags.label: Sensual
tone_tags.definition: Foregrounds tactile, physical, or sensory pleasure and attraction through image, sound, movement, or intimate presence.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from romantic: sensual concerns embodied desire and sensory experience, while romantic concerns love, longing, or idealized emotional attachment; either can occur without the other.

tone_tags.label: Candid
tone_tags.definition: Feels frank, emotionally exposed, or unguarded, presenting difficult experience or personal disclosure without protective polish or euphemism.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from earnest and gritty: earnest is sincerity of intent, and gritty is tactile realism of the depicted world; candid specifically describes openness and unvarnished disclosure.

tone_tags.label: Exuberant
tone_tags.definition: Expresses overflowing, high-energy joy, enthusiasm, or celebratory momentum that feels larger and more forceful than ordinary lightness.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from playful and uplifting: playful is mischievous in spirit, while uplifting describes the emotional trajectory or aftereffect; exuberant is the immediate intensity of joyful energy.

tone_tags.label: Nostalgic
tone_tags.definition: Looks backward with affection, longing, or idealization toward a remembered personal past, cultural moment, place, or style.
tone_tags.not: Distinct from melancholic and sentimental: nostalgia requires a backward-looking attachment, while melancholic names persistent sadness and sentimental names an overt emotion-eliciting technique.

tone_tag_preference_policy.version_note: The preference policy was introduced without a vocabulary change. Later ontology versions, including v0.3.0, may add controlled IDs while retaining the same zero-to-three field cardinality and the preference for exactly three genuinely descriptive tags.
tone_tag_preference_policy.summary: Prefer exactly 3 tone tags whenever three genuinely descriptive controlled tone terms apply. This reverses the prior default guidance ('prefer fewer, precise tags'), which is superseded wherever it appears in Pass 1/Pass 2 prompts and workflow docs.
rules: Prefer exactly 3 tone tags whenever three genuinely descriptive controlled tone terms apply.
2 tone tags are acceptable only when a third would be weak, redundant, speculative, or misleading.
1 or 0 tone tags should be rare and require genuinely insufficient evidence.
Never pad a title to 3 tags simply to satisfy the preferred count.
All tags must remain from the controlled tone vocabulary above.
tone_tag_preference_policy.does_not_apply_to: Historical Pass 1 and Pass 2 model outputs and final-classifications.json, which were produced under the prior guidance and are not retroactively altered by this policy. See curation/pilot/pass2/tone-coverage-review.json for the list of already-classified titles with fewer than 3 tone tags that a human editor may want to re-examine against this policy.

pacing.definition: Deliberately allows substantial time between major narrative developments; patience is a defining part of the viewing experience.
Neither deliberate patience nor sustained momentum is a defining characteristic.
Frequent narrative developments, action, jokes, revelations, scene changes, or escalating events create sustained forward momentum.

standup_design_principle: For content_type standup_special, primary_subgenre and secondary_subgenre must use the Stand-Up family. These fields describe the act's dominant comic construction or performance technique. Tone tags describe the audience-facing emotional or stylistic experience. Musical, impressions, storytelling, character, clean, and prop comedy are styles, not tones.
documentary_design_principle: Documentary-family IDs require a nonfiction form built from evidence such as interviews, observation, archival material, or reporting; a real subject alone does not make a work documentary. Use biographical-drama or true-crime-drama for scripted dramatizations, and concert-film when presenting a music performance is the work's primary purpose.
